title: The Defect Inspection Checklist: Utility vs. Aesthetic Realities
videoTitle: CHECK FOR DEFECTS IN YOUR PROPERTY
excerpt: A practical framework for inspecting newly handed-over homes: distinguishing essential utility defects from cosmetic flaws before starting renovation.
takeaways: Prioritise utility defects (water supply, piping, drainage, electrical circuits, and window locks) over cosmetic flaws.
Do not begin wet works or heavy renovations before officially lodging and rectifying defects with the developer.
Inspect common corridors, lift lobbies, and car park bays as they constitute shared strata ownership.

sections.heading: Utility defects vs cosmetic flaws
paragraphs: When taking vacant possession of a new home, excitement often leads owners to fixate on minor aesthetic imperfections like paint smudges or slight hairline plaster marks. Sean emphasises that the true priority must always be utility defects: water leakage, drainage blockages, uneven water pressure, faulty electrical wiring, and malfunctioning window latches.

While cosmetic blemishes are frustrating, utility failures can compromise living conditions, damage furniture, or create dangerous hazards. Categorising your inspection into functional essentials versus aesthetic tolerance ensures the developer addresses high-risk problems first.

sections.heading: The common area blind spot
paragraphs: A frequent mistake among strata property purchasers is limiting their inspection strictly within their own four walls. In Malaysia, your strata title gives you co-ownership of common property, including corridors, staircases, refuse chutes, and recreational facilities.

Sean encourages homeowners to check the condition of their designated parking bays, corridor tiles, and lift operations during the Defect Liability Period (DLP). Identifying shared water leaks or structural cracks early allows the Joint Management Body (JMB) to hold the developer accountable before the warranty window closes.

sections.heading: Why renovation timing matters
paragraphs: A critical warning highlighted in the guide is the temptation to rush into interior design and renovation immediately upon receiving the keys. If an owner commences hacking, tile replacement, or major carpentry before the developer rectifies defects, the developer may void warranty claims, arguing that damage was caused by third-party contractors.

Allowing the developer their stipulated rectification window (typically 30 days under the standard Housing Development Act schedule) provides a clean baseline. Once structural integrity and utilities are verified, interior renovation can proceed with total peace of mind.

closing: Prioritise function and safety over surface perfection. Resolving critical water and electrical defects early protects your renovation investment from day one.
sourceNote: Based on Sean Tan's published guide 'CHECK FOR DEFECTS IN YOUR PROPERTY' and Malaysian strata handover best practices.
